BERT4Rec already includes terminal masking: §3.6 adds training examples masking only the last item to reduce the mismatch with appended-[MASK] inference. The reference implementation mixes these examples into training; it does not implement a separate fine-tuning stage. For each window, it generates D random-mask copies plus one terminal-only copy, then shuffles them. With D=10, terminal-only examples constitute 1/11 of records. Random masking can also select the terminal position. Each real target has weight 1; run.py averages cross-entropy across all targets in the minibatch, so 1/11 of records does not imply 1/11 of loss weight. For constant k random targets/window, the explicit terminal-only contribution is approximately 1/(10k+1). [Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690), [generator](https://github.com/FeiSun/BERT4Rec/blob/master/gen_data_fin.py), [loss](https://github.com/FeiSun/BERT4Rec/blob/master/run.py).

Window generation is deterministic: histories no longer than N remain intact; longer histories produce length-N windows stepping backward from the latest window, plus a window starting at zero. There is no exhaustive prefix expansion or random prefix-length sampling. The ML-1m launcher uses N=200, stride=100, D=10, masking proportion 0.2, and all selected targets replaced by [MASK]. Masks are generated offline. [Generator](https://github.com/FeiSun/BERT4Rec/blob/master/gen_data_fin.py), [launcher](https://github.com/FeiSun/BERT4Rec/blob/master/run_ml-1m.sh).

The original paper does not report a controlled terminal-only versus random-only versus mixed ablation. Its “1 mask” comparison tests single-target Cloze versus multi-target Cloze and SASRec; mask-proportion sweeps vary target density. Neither isolates terminal masking. Thus adding terminal masking is established prior art; changing its frequency, weighting, or prefix sampling requires a controlled comparison to establish benefit. [Experiments](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690#S4).
